newsitem.title: USA: Senate leader raises possibility of no budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Senate leader raises possibility of no budget deal.

text.p: Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott warned President Clinton Thursday that progress must be made soon toward resolving budget differences or there just may not be a deal.
"Time is dwindling. If we don't begin to make some progress here in the next couple of weeks, I have my doubts frankly that we will be able to come to a budget agreement," Lott said.

"I've tried to keep the rhetoric lowered as much as possible on the president's budget proposal ... but the more I've looked at it, the less there is to it. There's just no 'there' there," the Mississippi Republican said.
It was the harshest comment so far to appear in the publicly stated goal to work in a bipartisan and conciliatory manner that marked the start of this Congress.

But that resolve has turned into partisan potshots recently with Republicans calling on Clinton to resubmit a budget they say does not achieve balance by 2002 as promised. The administration countered that the budget does reach balance under White House economic forecasts.
Both sides at the start of the year said they wanted to avoid the budget showdowns of the last Congress that resulted in two government shutdowns.
"I am not going to participate in a fraud. I am not going to walk out and say we're going to have a balanced budget ... if in fact that's not going to happen," Lott said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters during Clinton's trip to Lansing, Mich., that Congress must start to work on the budget that Clinton sent them.
"The key is for the president and the bipartisan leadership to sit down and go through the issues that would lead to a balanced budget by a certain date," McCurry said.

"And the most important thing that can happen at this point is for Congress to move seriously on the president's budget proposal, to mark it up and begin the work necessary to meet the statutory deadlines in the budget resolution," he added.
The April 15 deadline for the congressional budget resolution, which essentially is a blueprint for the budget, is likely to slip.
House Republican Leader Dick Armey, taking a more conciliatory tone than Lott, said a budget resolution was likely to reach the floor for a vote in May.

The Texas Republican urged patience with the White House because of the high changeover of officials there after the election. "There will be a budget that will be passed in this Congress and it will be in this session, this year, and it will be signed into law," Armey said.

Armey said he recently had discussions with White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles and believed the administration wanted to reach a balanced budget. "I believe he (Bowles) has a genuine honest resolve to get to a balanced budget, I think the White House has that," Armey said.

Republicans asked Clinton to resubmit his budget proposal, pointing to a Congressional Budget Office analysis that shows the government will still run a $69 billion deficit in 2002 unless extra spending cuts and tax increases come into play.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota pointed at Republicans as holding everything up because they were pushing for bigger tax cuts than Democrats wanted.
"It is time to begin serious negotiations, and one of the issues that will divide Republicans and Democrats for a while is this -- the Republican tax break proposal," Daschle said.
Clinton proposed $98 billion in tax cuts, while Senate Republicans were seeking double that amount.
The atmosphere became bitter in recent days as the White House lobbied Democrats to vote against a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution, which lost by one vote in the Senate Tuesday.
